Course Description

This course examines language variation in fictional film and television (primarily but not exclusively). You’ll analyze how media creators and consumers use language to signal social identities, create characters, engage narrative, and circulate ideas about society. You’ll learn how to think about language from a scientific perspective. You’ll use your creative, playful, and critical mind.

Course Approach

Most work happens during class time with my support. I expect roughly 3 hours of work outside class weekly, which will consist of about an hour working with readings, an hour selecting and preparing weekly clips and their metadata, 30 minutes watching team clips, and 30 minutes on things like class surveys/interviews.

Learning Outcomes

By course end, you will have:

  • Worked creatively, collaboratively, and critically
  • Improved your qualitative analysis abilities
  • Practiced curating media clips to illustrate concepts
  • Increased your power of observation
  • Created a team StoryMap showcasing language variation in media
  • Developed a scientific understanding of language variation
  • Gained experience with AI tools, including advanced prompting, evaluation of output, and using your own creativity to leverage what these tools can be good for and find out through experience where they really aren’t good or useful (hint: They are pretty bad, and quite time-consuming, for writing and editing that goes beyond the formulaic. We’ll talk about why that is in class)
  • Fostered real-world capacities: teamwork, presentations, giving/receiving feedback, audience design, attentiveness, and progressive mastery
  • Connected course concepts to your own experiences and social worlds

Assessment guidelines

Everyone who meets expectations earns an A. This is a progress- and learning-oriented course rather than one oriented around grades. You’ll get plenty of feedback but no grade. I’m here to help you succeed. No ‘gotchas,’ tricks, or hidden expectations. If something isn’t working, bring it up and we’ll work together to fix it.

  • Class Work: Active participation, prepared engagement, honest and respectful conversation, self/peer assessments
  • Group Clip Project: Weekly clip uploads, clip curation, team roles, final StoryMap. All teamwork will be done in class, so you shouldn’t need to meet outside of class

Detailed rubrics for individual and team-based expectations are available in Canvas.

Note: I’m there to help teams stay on track. Individual team members will be assessed based on the role they have (no overall team assessment)

Note: Being below expectations more than once triggers a progress discussion. Together, we’ll develop a plan for improvement.

Academic Integrity

Misconduct

As linguists and scientists, we all have an obligation to maintain ethical working practices that are open and honest (see the PRIME acronym for why this is important!) This includes, but is not limited to, upholding standards of integrity and honesty regarding the work that you present as your own. While there are many ways to incorporate uses of AI to help structure and plan your written work, it is neither honest, nor does it show academic integrity, to present the output of ChatGPT (among others) as your own, original work. Instances of AI dishonesty will be dealt with on a case-by-case basis, but if you are found to have submitted work that you have not produced yourself, you will most likely receive a grade of 0, and your case may be passed on to the Student Academic Affairs’ team. The same goes for submitting work that was produced by another human! Nobody wants that! If AI has been used in any process of your work (even very minor), this must be made explicit and be cited every time, with prompts and replies available upon request from the instructor.

Disability Accommodations

The University of Michigan recognizes disability as an integral part of diversity, equity and inclusion; and is committed to creating as accessible educational environment for students with disabilities/disabled students as possible.

Disability can include: mental health conditions, ADHD, learning disabilities, autism, chronic illness, physical conditions, sensory conditions, and more.

If you anticipate or are experiencing barriers based on disability or temporary injuries, Services for Students with Disabilities SSD is the office that students work with to explore reasonable accommodations, tools, and resources.

If you are already connected with SSD and have approved accommodations:

Please share your letter through Accommodate as soon as possible so that we can discuss how your accommodations will be implemented in this course. The sooner I know about your disability access needs, the more equipped I can be to facilitate accommodations. You may reach out to me or your Disability Access Coordinator if you have any questions or concerns about your accommodations.

If you have not connected with SSD:

If you anticipate or are experiencing a disability-related barrier and would like to discuss accommodations and/or resources, please contact SSD by completing their initial information form

For more information, call 734-763-3000 or email ssdoffice@umich.edu.

Mental Health & Wellbeing

The University of Michigan is committed to advancing the mental health and wellbeing of its students. If you or someone you know is feeling overwhelmed, depressed, and/or in need of support, services are available. For help, contact Counseling and Psychological Services (CAPS) at (734) 764-8312 during and after hours, on weekends and holidays, or through its counselors physically located in schools on both North and Central Campus. You may also consult University Health Service (UHS) at (734) 764-8320.

Discussions

The readings, class lectures, and my comments in class will suggest a particular point of view. This perspective is my own and does not have to be yours! I encourage you to disagree with the ideas in the readings and lectures as well as the perspectives of your colleagues in the course. Please express yourself! A significant part of a college education is learning about the complexity of various issues; therefore, it is important that we listen and respect one another but we do not have to agree. A richer discussion will occur when a variety of perspectives are presented in class for discussion.

Final notes

  • Course content: Material may at times include violence, substance use, sexual activity, or bigotry. I’ll provide warnings when needed. You may be uncomfortable (part of learning) but I’ll work to prevent distress.
  • Your voice matters: Course structure can be adjusted based on class feedback. We’re using new tools, and I want to know if they’re working.
  • A limited number of A+s will be given for performance that truly stands out. Only 1-2% of the class will get an A+, though no A+s are guaranteed
